title: Hair and evolution
paragraphs: Compared to other large mammals on Earth, we humans have relatively little hair. This obvious fact is not so strange until we look at our closest living relatives in the animal kingdom — chimpanzees and other great apes. Why, might we ask, have we evolved to be almost hairless when all other primates are still covered in fur? In fact, bizarre as it may seem, our lack of hair has been the key to our evolutionary success as a species.

The question why our earliest ancestors lost their hair when fur would have been beneficial to them — for keeping warm on cold nights, for example — was pondered by Charles Darwin, the famous evolutionist: "No one supposes that the nakedness of the skin is any direct advantage to man." He concluded that the reason hominins lost their hair was sexual selection. In other words, we prefer our partners to have little hair. But what caused our ancestors to start losing their hair before this preference set in?

The most likely hypothesis to explain the loss of hair is that it became necessary when early hominids moved to a more open savannah habitat around 2 to 3 million years ago, when they started to hunt big game. Hunting in open savannah meant being exposed to the strong heat of the sun for several hours in the day and being in danger of overheating. Being covered in hair prevented our ancestors from losing heat fast enough. So, as Peter Wheeler, of Liverpool John Moores University in the UK, explained, losing hair allowed them to develop the ability to sweat and therefore to cool down. Early humans could, as a consequence, be out at midday hunting and foraging. "It would be [an] enormous advantage to be able to spend the entire midday foraging, finding mates or fighting enemies", Tamás Dávid-Barrett of Oxford University says. "Sweating allows that, and for sweat to be efficient you need to be mostly hairless". The meat from hunting animals gave early humans the energy to fuel their growing brain.

Humans are the sweatiest primates on Earth. They have up to 5 million sweat glands, which produce about 12 litres of sweat per day. It's this propensity to sweat that accounts for our hairlessness and has allowed us to thrive. It might help to remember this next time you're surrounded by sweaty hairless torsos in the gym!

vocabulary.entry: evolve [v.] /ɪˈvɒlv/ 进化；演变 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: Humans evolved from earlier primates.
vocabulary.translation: 人类从早期的灵长类动物进化而来。

vocabulary.entry: primate [n.] /ˈpraɪmeɪt/ 灵长类动物
vocabulary.example: Gorillas are the largest primates.
vocabulary.translation: 大猩猩是最大的灵长类动物。

vocabulary.entry: bizarre [adj.] /bɪˈzɑː/ 离奇的；奇怪的
vocabulary.example: The painting was bizarre and colourful.
vocabulary.translation: 这幅画离奇而色彩丰富。

vocabulary.entry: hominin [n.] /ˈhɒmɪnɪn/ 人科动物（包括人类及其已灭绝的近亲）(专业词汇)
vocabulary.example: Hominins walked upright on two legs.
vocabulary.translation: 人科动物用两条腿直立行走。

vocabulary.entry: hypothesis [n.] /haɪˈpɒθəsɪs/ 假设；假说 (书面语；复数: hypotheses)
vocabulary.example: The hypothesis was supported by evidence.
vocabulary.translation: 这个假设得到了证据的支持。

vocabulary.entry: hominid [n.] /ˈhɒmɪnɪd/ 原始人类；人科动物 (专业词汇)
vocabulary.example: Hominids lived millions of years ago.
vocabulary.translation: 原始人类生活在数百万年前。

vocabulary.entry: forage [v.] /ˈfɒrɪdʒ/ 觅食；搜寻
vocabulary.example: The bears foraged for berries in the forest.
vocabulary.translation: 熊在森林里觅食浆果。

vocabulary.entry: propensity [n.] /prəˈpensəti/ 倾向；习性 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: He has a propensity to talk too much.
vocabulary.translation: 他有话太多的倾向。

vocabulary.entry: thrive [v.] /θraɪv/ 茁壮成长；兴旺 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: The business thrived under new management.
vocabulary.translation: 这家企业在新管理下蓬勃发展。

vocabulary.entry: compared to [phr.] /kəmˈpeəd tuː/ 与……相比 (固定搭配)
vocabulary.example: Compared to London, Paris is smaller.
vocabulary.translation: 与伦敦相比，巴黎更小。

vocabulary.entry: be covered in [phr.] /biː ˈkʌvəd ɪn/ 被……覆盖 (固定搭配)
vocabulary.example: The mountains are covered in snow.
vocabulary.translation: 山上覆盖着雪。

vocabulary.entry: ponder [v.] /ˈpɒndə/ 思考；沉思 (书面语)
vocabulary.example: He pondered the question for a long time.
vocabulary.translation: 他思考这个问题很久了。

vocabulary.entry: sexual selection [n.] /ˈsekʃuəl sɪˈlekʃən/ 性选择 (专业词汇)
vocabulary.example: Peacocks' tails are a result of sexual selection.
vocabulary.translation: 孔雀的尾巴是性选择的结果。

vocabulary.entry: set in [phr.] /set ɪn/ 开始；到来 (固定搭配)
vocabulary.example: Winter has set in early this year.
vocabulary.translation: 今年冬天来得很早。

vocabulary.example: Workers are exposed to harmful chemicals.
vocabulary.translation: 工人们接触到有害化学物质。

vocabulary.translation: 这个物种有灭绝的危险。

vocabulary.entry: account for [phr.] /əˈkaʊnt fɔː/ 解释；占……比例 (固定搭配)
vocabulary.example: How do you account for your absence?
vocabulary.translation: 你如何解释你的缺席？

vocabulary.entry: sweat gland [n.] /swet ɡlænd/ 汗腺 (生物学词汇)
vocabulary.example: Sweat glands help regulate body temperature.
vocabulary.translation: 汗腺有助于调节体温。

vocabulary.entry: fuel [v.] /ˈfjuːəl/ 给……提供能量；推动
vocabulary.example: Protein fuels muscle growth.
vocabulary.translation: 蛋白质为肌肉生长提供能量。

vocabulary.entry: torso [n.] /ˈtɔːsəʊ/ 躯干 (复数: torsos)
vocabulary.example: The statue has a muscular torso.
vocabulary.translation: 这座雕像有肌肉发达的躯干。

sentences.english: Compared to other large mammals on Earth, we humans have relatively little hair.
sentences.chinese: 与地球上的其他大型哺乳动物相比，我们人类的毛发相对较少。

sentences.english: This obvious fact is not so strange until we look at our closest living relatives in the animal kingdom — chimpanzees and other great apes.
sentences.chinese: 这个显而易见的事实并没有什么奇怪的，直到我们看到动物王国中与我们关系最密切的现存近亲——黑猩猩和其他大型猿类。

sentences.english: Why, might we ask, have we evolved to be almost hairless when all other primates are still covered in fur?
sentences.chinese: 我们不禁要问，为什么当所有其他灵长类动物仍然浑身覆盖着毛发时，我们却进化得几乎没有毛发了呢？

sentences.english: In fact, bizarre as it may seem, our lack of hair has been the key to our evolutionary success as a species.
sentences.chinese: 事实上，尽管这可能看起来很离奇，但我们毛发的缺失却是我们作为一个物种在进化上取得成功的关键。

sentences.english: The question why our earliest ancestors lost their hair when fur would have been beneficial to them — for keeping warm on cold nights, for example — was pondered by Charles Darwin, the famous evolutionist: "No one supposes that the nakedness of the skin is any direct advantage to man."
sentences.chinese: 我们最早的祖先为什么会在毛发对他们有益的时候（比如在寒冷的夜晚保暖）失去毛发，这个问题曾被著名的进化论者查尔斯·达尔文思考过：“没有人认为皮肤裸露对人类有任何直接的好处。”

sentences.english: He concluded that the reason hominins lost their hair was sexual selection.
sentences.chinese: 他得出的结论是，原始人类失去毛发的原因是性选择。

sentences.english: In other words, we prefer our partners to have little hair.
sentences.chinese: 换句话说，我们更倾向于选择毛发较少的伴侣。

sentences.english: But what caused our ancestors to start losing their hair before this preference set in?
sentences.chinese: 但是，是什么导致我们的祖先在这种偏好形成之前就开始失去毛发了呢？

sentences.english: The most likely hypothesis to explain the loss of hair is that it became necessary when early hominids moved to a more open savannah habitat around 2 to 3 million years ago, when they started to hunt big game.
sentences.chinese: 解释毛发缺失最有可能的假设是，大约在200万到300万年前，早期原始人类迁移到更开阔的草原栖息地，开始捕猎大型猎物时，毛发的缺失就变得有必要了。

sentences.english: Hunting in open savannah meant being exposed to the strong heat of the sun for several hours in the day and being in danger of overheating.
sentences.chinese: 在开阔的草原上狩猎意味着每天要暴露在强烈的阳光下几个小时，并且有过热的危险。

sentences.english: Being covered in hair prevented our ancestors from losing heat fast enough.
sentences.chinese: 浑身覆盖着毛发会阻碍我们的祖先足够快地散热。

sentences.english: So, as Peter Wheeler, of Liverpool John Moores University in the UK, explained, losing hair allowed them to develop the ability to sweat and therefore to cool down.
sentences.chinese: 所以，正如英国利物浦约翰摩尔大学的彼得·惠勒所解释的那样，失去毛发使他们能够发展出汗的能力，从而降温。

sentences.english: Early humans could, as a consequence, be out at midday hunting and foraging.
sentences.chinese: 因此，早期人类可以在正午时分外出狩猎和觅食。

sentences.english: "It would be [an] enormous advantage to be able to spend the entire midday foraging, finding mates or fighting enemies", Tamás Dávid-Barrett of Oxford University says.
sentences.chinese: 牛津大学的塔马斯·大卫－巴雷特说：“能够在整个正午时分觅食、寻找伴侣或与敌人战斗，这将是一个巨大的优势。”

sentences.english: "Sweating allows that, and for sweat to be efficient you need to be mostly hairless".
sentences.chinese: “出汗使这成为可能，而且为了让出汗更有效率，你需要几乎没有毛发。”

sentences.english: The meat from hunting animals gave early humans the energy to fuel their growing brain.
sentences.chinese: 狩猎动物获得的肉为早期人类提供了能量，促进了他们大脑的发育。

sentences.english: Humans are the sweatiest primates on Earth.
sentences.chinese: 人类是地球上出汗最多的灵长类动物。

sentences.english: They have up to 5 million sweat glands, which produce about 12 litres of sweat per day.
sentences.chinese: 人类拥有多达500万个汗腺，每天大约能产生12升汗水。

sentences.english: It's this propensity to sweat that accounts for our hairlessness and has allowed us to thrive.
sentences.chinese: 正是这种出汗的倾向解释了我们毛发缺失的原因，并使我们得以繁衍兴旺。

sentences.english: It might help to remember this next time you're surrounded by sweaty hairless torsos in the gym!
sentences.chinese: 下次当你在健身房里被汗流浃背、没有毛发的身躯包围时，记住这一点可能会有所帮助！
